q: A Gulf Coast shelter intakes 14 feral cats. Which statement correctly differentiates endoparasite transmission dynamics in the shelter?
o: Dirofilaria immitis spreads cage-to-cage via aerosolized respiratory droplets
Direct-transmission parasites like Giardia and Cryptosporidium are immediately infective when shed, enabling rapid fomite spread
Toxocara and coccidia are instantly infective on excretion, so sanitation cannot help
Indirect parasites cause widespread outbreaks even without their vector
e: Giardia and Cryptosporidium are shed already infective; Toxocara/coccidia need environmental development; indirect parasites need their vector.

q: An asymptomatic 2-year-old cat is heartworm antigen-positive at intake. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the canine three-dose melarsomine protocol
Surgically extract worms via the jugular as first-line for all positive cats
Avoid adulticide (melarsomine is unsafe in cats), manage supportively and monitor, and counsel adopters about the real risk of acute decompensation
Permanently isolate the cat from other cats to prevent direct cat-to-cat worm transmission
e: Melarsomine is not recommended in cats; manage supportively. Feline heartworm can cause sudden death, so adopters need honest counseling.

q: A Midwest ferret has lethargy, open-mouth breathing, muddy-blue mucous membranes, and bilirubinuria. Most likely diagnosis?
o: Sarcoptes scabiei anaphylaxis
Heartworm disease, even with a low adult worm burden
Quaternary ammonium disinfectant toxicosis
Trichodectes canis-induced anemia
e: Ferrets are exquisitely susceptible; even one worm can obstruct the tiny heart, and bilirubinuria is the most consistently reported clinicopathologic change.

q: Why is a heartworm antigen test prone to false-negatives in a ferret with clear right-sided heart failure?
o: Ferrets cannot make antibodies against microfilariae
Ferret red cells denature heartworm antigens within 2 hours
Ferrets often harbor very low burdens or single-sex (male) infections, so antigen falls below detection
Antigen tests cross-react with Demodex proteins
e: Antigen tests detect adult female antigen; low burdens or male-only infections drop the antigenic load below the detection threshold.

q: A 3-week-old orphan puppy has a heavy flea infestation and is too young for most systemic products. Safest validated plan?
o: Concentrated organophosphate garden-insecticide dip
Fipronil-based spray (noted safe for neonatal kittens and puppies), with mechanical flea combing and warmth as adjuncts
High-dose oral ivermectin plus a sulfur dip
A 45% permethrin spot-on for extra-large dogs at a micro-dose
e: Fipronil spray is the safe, validated option for neonates; mechanical removal and warmth matter, and the other options risk fatal neurotoxicity.

q: Twelve dogs in a hoarding case have pruritus and hyperkeratosis on the ventrum, pinnae, and elbows; scraping confirms Sarcoptes scabiei var. canis. Required measure?
o: No isolation, since Sarcoptes is strictly host-specific
Immediate isolation and PPE due to high cross-contagion and zoonotic potential for staff
House affected dogs in the feline ward
Bathe in cow's milk and withhold macrocyclic lactones until age 2
e: Canine scabies is highly contagious and zoonotic; isolate and use PPE for the first 3 to 5 days of treatment.

q: An asymptomatic Pit Bull mix is PCR-positive for Babesia gibsoni and completes triple antibiotic therapy. What must adopters be told?
o: The dog is fully cured and needs no preventives
Therapy reduces parasitemia but does not clear the organism; the dog is a permanent subclinical carrier needing lifelong tick prevention
The dog is contagious to humans via saliva and must be euthanized
The dog will develop right-sided heart failure if it meets a cat
e: B. gibsoni is rarely cleared; treated dogs remain carriers at risk of relapse and need lifelong tick prevention (atovaquone-azithromycin is the more effective protocol).

q: An 11-day-old stray-litter puppy has mucosal pallor, lethargy, and tarry feces, with high hookworm egg counts on flotation. How did patent infection arise so early?
o: Percutaneous L3 penetration 24 hours earlier
Transmammary transmission of A. caninum via milk, with a ~2-week prepatent period allowing egg shedding and anemia by 14 days
Ingestion of an infected rodent in the whelping box
Mutation of gut flora into hookworm oocysts
e: A. caninum is transmitted in the bitch's milk; its ~2-week prepatent period lets neonates shed eggs and become anemic by ~14 days.

q: Dogs in a Texas outdoor pen develop acute myocarditis and right-sided cardiomegaly. Which vector and mechanism should biosecurity target?
o: Ixodes ticks injecting the pathogen in saliva
Triatomine (kissing) bugs depositing infective stages in feces near the bite, or being ingested by the dog
Anopheles mosquitoes transmitting microfilariae
Rodent nests aerosolizing Francisella tularensis
e: Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas) is spread by triatomine bugs via fecal (stercorarian) contamination of the bite or by ingestion of the bug.

q: A feline-only shelter has juvenile cats with intense pruritus and scaling on heads and faces; scraping shows a sarcoptid mite. Organism and transmissibility?
o: Demodex gatoi, strictly non-contagious, no zoonotic risk
Notoedres cati, highly contagious among cats with zoonotic potential for staff
Linognathus setosus, a sucking louse of dogs only
Cheyletiella, which only infests rabbits
e: Notoedres cati (feline scabies) starts on the head and face, is highly contagious among cats, and is zoonotic.

q: What is the ASV intake mandate for intestinal parasites in dogs and cats?
o: Treat only animals with diarrhea
Treat all dogs and cats for roundworms and hookworms at intake, starting at 2 weeks of age, because of zoonotic risk
Treat for whipworms and tapeworms first, since they are most dangerous
Delay all deworming until after the stray hold
e: All dogs and cats must be treated for roundworms and hookworms at intake from 2 weeks of age due to the zoonotic risk.

q: Why should a broad-spectrum heartworm and flea spot-on not replace a primary dewormer at intake?
o: Spot-ons are more expensive than tablets
They should not be used in place of a primary deworming product effective against hookworms and roundworms
They are illegal in shelters
They only work on cats
e: Broad-spectrum parasiticide spot-ons should not substitute for a primary hookworm-and-roundworm dewormer.

q: Which drug covers hookworms, roundworms, whipworms, and Giardia, but NOT Dipylidium or Echinococcus?
o: Praziquantel
Fenbendazole
Pyrantel pamoate alone
Selamectin
e: Fenbendazole (50 mg/kg PO for 3 to 5 days) is broad but misses Dipylidium and Echinococcus; praziquantel is used for those.

q: Which statement about parasite egg environmental persistence is correct?
o: Hookworm eggs are the hardiest and survive years on dry surfaces
Ascarid eggs are extremely resistant and become nearly impossible to destroy once in soil, whereas hookworm eggs are killed fairly rapidly by desiccation
All parasite eggs are killed instantly by routine disinfectants
Whipworm eggs cannot survive outside the host
e: Ascarid eggs are highly resistant (impossible to clear from soil); hookworm eggs are fragile and desiccate readily on dry surfaces.

q: For nematode infections detected at intake, what is the recommended approach to isolation?
o: Strict isolation of all infected animals for 30 days
No need to isolate or quarantine, because the eggs are not immediately infective; prioritize prompt post-treatment sanitation
Euthanize to prevent environmental contamination
Quarantine only the cats
e: Ascarid/hookworm/whipworm eggs are not immediately infective, so no isolation is needed; thorough post-treatment cleanup is the priority.

q: Which roundworm is the deadliest zoonotic agent, causing fatal neural larva migrans in humans?
o: Toxocara canis
Toxascaris leonina
Baylisascaris procyonis
Toxocara cati
e: Baylisascaris procyonis (raccoon ascarid) causes severe, often fatal neural larva migrans; T. canis is the most common cause of larva migrans overall.

q: Which hookworm species causes the majority of cutaneous larva migrans cases in the US?
o: Ancylostoma caninum
Ancylostoma braziliense
Uncinaria stenocephala
Ancylostoma tubaeforme
e: A. braziliense lingers in the dermis and causes most human cutaneous larva migrans cases.

q: What is the diagnostic test of choice for intestinal nematode eggs?
o: Direct saline smear only
Zinc sulfate centrifugation fecal examination
Blood antigen test
Urine sediment cytology
e: Zinc sulfate centrifugation is the test of choice; intermittent shedding means a single negative does not rule out infection.

q: How is Dipylidium caninum most effectively controlled in a shelter?
o: Strict isolation of infected animals
A robust flea-control program, since the flea is its intermediate host
Routine fenbendazole for all animals
Environmental bleach alone
e: Dipylidium uses the flea as its intermediate host, so good flea control prevents it; visible segments mean flea control needs review.

q: For Toxocara canis, which transmission route allows puppies to be infected before birth?
o: Percutaneous only
Transplacental (in utero) transmission, so pups can shed eggs by about 3 weeks of age
Fomite transmission via bedding
There is no vertical transmission of T. canis
e: T. canis crosses the placenta; in-utero-infected pups can shed eggs by ~3 weeks despite a ~5-week prepatent period after egg ingestion.

q: Which best characterizes whipworm (Trichuris vulpis)?
o: A flea-borne tapeworm with high zoonotic risk
A direct-life-cycle nematode of the cecum and colon with a ~3-month prepatent period and a barrel-shaped bipolar-plugged egg
An obligate intermediate-host parasite
A protozoan diagnosed by ELISA only
e: Trichuris vulpis has a direct cycle, ~3-month prepatent period, lives in cecum/colon, and has a hardy barrel-shaped bipolar-plugged egg.

q: After deworming a heavily infected dog, why is prompt sanitation critical?
o: The dewormer makes the dog contagious by air
The feces will contain massive numbers of eggs that can contaminate the environment
The dog must be isolated for 30 days
Eggs become airborne after treatment
e: Post-treatment feces shed huge egg numbers; prompt, thorough cleanup prevents environmental contamination.

q: A cat presents with diarrhea. What is the appropriate diagnostic sequence before empiric treatment?
o: Immediate euthanasia
Fecal flotation, direct smear and cytology, and a Giardia ELISA as needed; if negative, treat with a broad-spectrum anthelmintic
Blood heartworm antigen test only
Skin scrape
e: Work up feline diarrhea with flotation, direct smear/cytology, and Giardia ELISA; treat empirically with a broad-spectrum dewormer if negative.

q: Per the AAFP/ASV guidelines, what is the recommended minimum diagnostic plan for acute diarrhea?
o: Fecal flotation plus a Giardia antigen assay
Abdominal radiographs only
Empiric metronidazole with no testing
PCR panel as the sole first-line test
e: The AAFP/ASV minimum diagnostic plan for acute diarrhea is fecal flotation plus a Giardia antigen (Ag) assay; cysts shed intermittently, so antigen testing complements flotation.

q: A shelter dog has Giardia-associated diarrhea. What is the preferred first-line treatment, and why is metronidazole not first choice?
o: Metronidazole 25 mg/kg q12h, because it is far more effective than fenbendazole
Fenbendazole 50 mg/kg q24h for 5 days plus environmental control; metronidazole has equivalent efficacy but causes dysbiosis and is linked to chronic GI signs, especially in juveniles
Praziquantel once, because Giardia is a tapeworm
No treatment is ever indicated because Giardia is harmless
e: Fenbendazole 50 mg/kg q24h x5d plus environmental control is adequate. A 2021 RCT showed no significant efficacy difference vs metronidazole (P=0.686), but metronidazole disrupts the microbiome and is linked to chronic intestinal signs in juveniles; persistent cases get a repeat fenbendazole cycle, not a drug switch.

q: Why can a quaternary ammonium disinfectant fail to control a Giardia outbreak in a shelter ward?
o: Quats evaporate too quickly to contact the floor
Giardia cysts are resistant to quaternary ammonium compounds; effective measures are thorough drying, steam/heat, accelerated hydrogen peroxide, or bleach on hard surfaces
Quats only work on enveloped viruses, and Giardia is an enveloped virus
Cysts are killed only by quats, so the ward was under-dosed
e: Giardia cysts resist QACs. Because cysts are immediately infective and persist in moisture, control relies on prompt feces removal, fixing drainage/standing water, and drying, steam, or accelerated H2O2 (e.g. Oxivir) rather than quats.

q: What does a commercial heartworm antigen test actually detect, and how are microfilariae detected?
o: It detects microfilariae directly; adults are found by ELISA
It detects circulating antigen of adult female worms; microfilariae are detected by concentration tests such as the Modified Knott
It detects larval L3 in the skin; adults are found on radiographs
It detects Wolbachia DNA; microfilariae are found by antigen test
e: Antigen tests detect adult female worm antigen; microfilariae are found by concentration tests (Modified Knott), which is why both tests are run.

q: At what minimum age should dogs be screened for heartworm, and why?
o: 6 weeks, because larvae are present at birth
About 7 months, because the prepatent period is roughly 6 months
12 months, because antigen appears only in adults over a year old
Any age, since tests detect L3 immediately
e: Do not test before about 7 months; the ~6-month prepatent period means earlier testing wastes resources.

q: A dog on preventives is antigen-negative but heartworm is strongly suspected. What technique can unmask antigen?
o: Repeating the same in-clinic test twice
Heat treatment of the serum sample to break antigen-antibody complexes
Switching to a microfilaria smear only
Waiting 2 years and retesting
e: Heat treatment of serum breaks antigen-antibody complexes and can convert a false-negative to a true positive.

q: Which describes the AHS-preferred adulticidal protocol?
o: Macrocyclic-lactone-only slow kill for all dogs
Doxycycline plus a macrocyclic lactone, then the three-dose melarsomine protocol (one dose, then two doses 24 hours apart about a month later)
A single melarsomine injection with no doxycycline
Surgical extraction as the routine first-line treatment
e: AHS recommends doxycycline and an ML, then three-dose melarsomine; the three-dose protocol is safest and ~99% effective.

q: What is the role of doxycycline in heartworm treatment?
o: It is the adulticide of choice
It suppresses Wolbachia, reduces post-treatment pulmonary pathology and microfilarial counts, and renders microfilariae non-infective to mosquitoes
It replaces the need for exercise restriction
It is given only to cats
e: Doxycycline (10 mg/kg BID x 28 days) targets the Wolbachia endosymbiont, cutting pathology and transmission.

q: When is a macrocyclic-lactone-only 'slow-kill' approach appropriate?
o: As the routine first choice for all shelter dogs
Only when melarsomine is contraindicated or unavailable (for example anaphylaxis to melarsomine or a grave non-heartworm prognosis), and not in dogs that cannot be exercise-restricted
Whenever the dog has caval syndrome
For performance dogs to keep them working
e: Slow-kill is not recommended except in specific situations; it is contraindicated in performance dogs and those that cannot be activity-restricted.

q: A heavily infected dog acutely develops collapse from worms obstructing the tricuspid valve. What is this, and the prognosis?
o: Caval syndrome, usually fatal within about 2 days unless worms are surgically extracted
Simple pulmonary hypertension, resolves with rest
Anaphylaxis to doxycycline, self-limiting
Microfilarial dermatitis, treated topically
e: Caval syndrome is acute tricuspid obstruction by worms, usually fatal within ~2 days without prompt surgical extraction.

q: What does the ASV Heartworm Management position statement (2024) recommend for shelter prevention?
o: Prevention only during summer in endemic states
Year-round heartworm prevention for dogs, cats, and ferrets, since some transmission risk exists everywhere
Prevention only for dogs that test positive
No prevention until adoption
e: The ASV urges year-round prevention for dogs, cats, and ferrets because transmission risk exists year-round regardless of geography.

q: A shelter cannot afford to treat a heartworm-positive dog. What does the ASV position statement support?
o: Mandatory euthanasia of all positive dogs
Transfer to a partner with treatment capacity, or release to an informed adopter with clear follow-up expectations
Indefinite housing without prevention
Withholding the diagnosis from adopters
e: The ASV supports transfer to a capable partner or informed-adopter release with follow-up, and notes resources should not be diverted from other animals.

q: How do sucking lice (Anoplura) differ structurally from chewing lice (Mallophaga)?
o: Sucking lice have a head wider than the thorax
Sucking lice have a head about as wide as the thorax and feed on blood, while chewing lice have a head wider than the thorax and eat skin debris
They are indistinguishable without PCR
Chewing lice suck blood; sucking lice eat debris
e: Anoplura (blood-sucking) have a head about as wide as the thorax; Mallophaga (chewing) have a head wider than the thorax.

q: Which statement about Demodex is correct?
o: All Demodex species are highly contagious between dogs and cats
Demodex is generally non-contagious (acquired from the dam while nursing); generalized demodicosis reflects immunosuppression and is heritable, and isoxazolines are often the treatment of choice
Demodex has no host specificity
Amitraz is the only effective option and isoxazolines do not work
e: Demodex is host-specific and generally non-contagious; generalized disease signals immunosuppression, is heritable, and isoxazolines are now often preferred.

q: How are fleas most commonly acquired, and which stage is hardiest?
o: Adult fleas jumping directly from one animal to another; the egg is hardiest
From a contaminated environment where eggs, larvae, and pupae have developed; the pupa is the hardiest stage and persists for months
Only by ingestion of infected prey; the larva is hardiest
By aerosol; the adult is hardiest
e: Animals pick up fleas from the environment, not host-to-host; the pupa is the hardiest stage, persisting for months awaiting a host.

q: What distinguishes primary from secondary myiasis?
o: Primary myiasis only affects cats

Primary myiasis (for example the reportable screwworm Cochliomyia hominivorax) requires living tissue, whereas secondary myiasis is opportunistic invasion of devitalized tissue on soiled or wounded animals
Secondary myiasis is always fatal
They are the same condition
e: Primary myiasis needs living tissue (screwworm is reportable); secondary myiasis is opportunistic on devitalized tissue of debilitated animals.

q: Which pathogen is correctly paired with its vector?
o: Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme) transmitted by fleas
Bartonella spp. transmitted by ticks only
Rickettsia rickettsii (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) transmitted by ticks
Yersinia pestis (plague) transmitted by sandflies
e: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii) is tick-borne; Lyme is tick-borne, Bartonella is flea-associated, and plague is flea/aerosol.

q: Which arthropods have strict host specificity and so cannot establish infestation across different host species?
o: Fleas and ticks
Only lice and Demodex mites
Mosquitoes and sandflies
All mites and all lice
e: Only lice and Demodex mites are strictly host-specific; all other arthropods of concern are opportunistic feeders.

q: A shelter wants to reduce environmental vector burden. Which measure is most appropriate?
o: Routinely use footbaths as the primary control
Remove standing water, garbage, decaying organic matter, and long grass to limit vector breeding
House all animals outdoors to dilute exposure
Stop tick prevention to avoid resistance
e: Eliminating standing water, refuse, decaying matter, and long grass reduces vector breeding sites around the shelter.

q: A 10-month-old shelter cat has had intermittent large-bowel diarrhea (fresh blood, mucus, tenesmus) for 6 weeks but is bright and eating well. Which pathogen is most consistent with this presentation?
o: Toxocara cati (roundworm)
Tritrichomonas foetus
Cryptosporidium felis
Dirofilaria immitis
e: T. foetus causes chronic large-bowel diarrhea with normal systemic signs in young cats in congregate settings. Cryptosporidium affects the small bowel. Toxocara and heartworm present differently.

q: A direct fecal smear on a symptomatic cat reveals motile, pear-shaped organisms. Which morphologic feature best distinguishes Tritrichomonas foetus from Giardia?
o: Two nuclei (owl-eyes) and a concave ventral disc
One nucleus, a visible axostyle (stiff posterior rod), and a forward rolling movement
Backward tumbling ('falling leaf') motility and multiple flagella
Absence of any motility with refractile walls
e: T. foetus has one nucleus and a prominent axostyle with forward rolling movement. Giardia has two nuclei (owl-eye appearance), a concave ventral disc, and falling-leaf motility.

q: Which treatment is effective for Tritrichomonas foetus infection in cats?
o: Metronidazole 25 mg/kg PO BID × 7 days
Ronidazole 30 mg/kg PO once daily × 14 days
Fenbendazole 50 mg/kg PO × 5 days
Praziquantel 5 mg/kg PO single dose
e: Ronidazole is the drug of choice for T. foetus. Metronidazole has poor efficacy against Tritrichomonas and will NOT resolve the infection — a high-frequency exam trap.

q: Which statement about Tritrichomonas foetus in shelter cats is correct?
o: It is transmitted by fleas and requires immediate adulticide treatment
Transmission is fecal-oral via shared litter boxes; many cats will self-cure over months to years without treatment
It responds to standard metronidazole treatment given for 5 days
It exclusively causes small bowel diarrhea with vomiting and weight loss
e: T. foetus is fecal-oral via litter box contamination and causes large-bowel diarrhea; many cats self-cure, making ronidazole for shortening the course rather than a cure-or-die necessity.

q: Which disinfectant is most commonly used in shelters but FAILS against Cryptosporidium oocysts?
o: 6% hydrogen peroxide
Steam cleaning over 60°C (140°F)
Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) at standard dilutions
Desiccation (drying)
e: Cryptosporidium oocysts are highly resistant to chlorine. Bleach at standard shelter dilutions does NOT reliably kill them. This is a critical practical exam trap — steam and high-concentration H₂O₂ are needed.

q: A shelter cat is diagnosed with Cryptosporidium felis infection. Regarding transmission timing, which statement is correct?
o: Oocysts require a 1–2 week sporulation period before becoming infective
Oocysts are immediately infective when shed — no external development required
Oocysts can only be transmitted through an arthropod vector
Oocysts require ingestion by a rodent intermediate host before infecting cats
e: Cryptosporidium oocysts are immediately infective when shed (autoinfective sporulated oocysts), enabling rapid fecal-oral spread without any external development period.

q: The recommended staining technique for detecting Cryptosporidium oocysts on fecal smear is:
o: Gram stain
Modified Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain — oocysts stain pink-red
Giemsa stain
Romanowsky stain
e: Modified Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain is the reference method; oocysts stain pink to red against a blue-green background. Routine fecal flotation has poor sensitivity because oocysts are very small (~4–5 μm).

q: Which statement about zoonotic risk from Cryptosporidium in a shelter is correct?
o: Only C. felis poses significant zoonotic risk to humans
C. parvum is the most important zoonotic species; immunocompromised staff are at high risk; handwashing is the primary protective measure
Cryptosporidium poses no zoonotic risk when the animal shows no clinical signs
Zoonotic risk is eliminated by standard bleach disinfection of kennels
e: C. parvum is a significant human pathogen, especially for immunocompromised individuals. Bleach fails against oocysts, so handwashing and steam/H₂O₂ disinfection are essential safeguards.

q: An adult shelter dog (3 years old) develops diffuse alopecia and skin thickening with deep scrape confirming generalized Demodex canis. What is the most appropriate next step after initiating treatment?
o: Dismiss as cosmetic; no further workup needed

Investigate for underlying systemic disease (hypothyroidism, hyperadrenocorticism, neoplasia, or immunosuppressive drugs), because adult-onset generalized demodicosis is always a flag for an underlying cause
Quarantine the dog as highly contagious and contact trace all kennel neighbors
Recommend euthanasia due to the heritable nature of all demodicosis cases
e: Adult-onset generalized demodicosis (>18 months) requires investigation of an underlying cause. Juvenile-onset (<18 months) is heritable; adult-onset is acquired due to immunosuppression from systemic disease or drugs.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes Demodex canis from Demodex gatoi regarding contagiousness?
o: Both species are non-contagious and only passed from dam to offspring
D. canis is highly contagious between dogs; D. gatoi is non-contagious
D. canis is non-contagious except dam-to-pup during nursing; D. gatoi IS contagious between cats
Both species are zoonotic and require strict isolation
e: D. canis is NOT contagious between adult dogs (only transmitted dam-to-pup while nursing). D. gatoi IS contagious between cats. This distinction is a high-frequency exam trap.

q: Which treatment is now considered first-line for generalized Demodex canis in a shelter dog?
o: Amitraz whole-body dips every 2 weeks (FDA-approved protocol)
Daily oral ivermectin in all breeds
Isoxazolines (fluralaner, afoxolaner, sarolaner, or lotilaner) — simple, effective, monthly or single-dose oral treatment
Lime sulfur dips as for ringworm
e: Isoxazolines are now the treatment of choice for generalized demodicosis: easy to administer, highly effective, safe. Amitraz remains FDA-approved but is labor-intensive and has toxicity concerns for staff. Ivermectin is effective but not FDA-approved and risky in MDR1-affected breeds.

q: A 6-month-old shelter dog develops generalized demodicosis. Which action is critical before adoption beyond starting treatment?
o: No additional action beyond treating the mites
Neuter the dog before adoption, because juvenile-onset generalized demodicosis indicates a heritable immune defect that should not be passed to offspring
Place in permanent isolation as all demodicosis is highly contagious
Start lifelong immunosuppressive therapy to manage the immune defect
e: Juvenile-onset generalized demodicosis indicates a heritable T-cell immune defect. Neuter before adoption and counsel the adopter not to breed related animals.

q: A serosurvey of 552 Australian feral and stray cats found approximately 40% seropositive for Toxoplasma gondii. What does this level of seroprevalence imply for public health and wildlife conservation?
o: Low risk, as most cats clear infection before shedding environmentally viable oocysts
Significant environmental oocyst contamination risk given that cats are the only definitive host in Australia capable of shedding oocysts
Moderate risk limited to urban areas where stray cats contact humans directly
Negligible risk because T. gondii in Australia affects only wildlife, not humans or livestock
e: In Australia, cats are the only definitive host for T. gondii capable of shedding oocysts. A 40% seroprevalence across a large free-roaming population represents a substantial environmental contamination risk for wildlife, livestock, and humans — the core public health concern the paper raises.

q: Among the risk factors examined for T. gondii seropositivity in Australian feral and stray cats, which was notably NOT significant?
o: Bodyweight (used as a proxy for age)
Geographical location
Sex (male vs. female)
Whether the cat was feral vs. stray
e: Sex was not a significant risk factor. Significant predictors included bodyweight (proxy for age — older cats more likely exposed), geographical location, season, and feral vs. stray status. The absence of a sex effect means both sexes require equal consideration in public health risk assessment.

q: An in-house modified agglutination test (MAT) was developed and compared to a commercial MAT in this study. What was the practical significance of this methodological development?
o: The in-house MAT was less sensitive, limiting its use to screening only
The in-house MAT provided a reliable and economical serological tool where commercial kits are inaccessible
The in-house MAT detected IgM antibodies, enabling acute infection identification unlike the commercial kit
The two tests showed only moderate agreement, so both should be run in parallel
e: The in-house MAT showed excellent agreement with the commercial MAT and was developed specifically because commercial kits are not easily accessible in Australia. This makes large-scale, cost-effective screening feasible — important for epidemiological surveillance in resource-limited settings.
